summary: Describes the operating model of Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN product, which uses virtual LANs to decide whether connection requests are allowed and to limit broadcasts. It is a vendor description published as informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2643 describes how Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN switches worked. Rather than looking at each packet on its own, a switch sets up a connection for each pair of addresses it sees, and the hardware then forwards matching packets by itself. Virtual LANs decide which connections are allowed and keep broadcast traffic inside the right group.

questions: how do vlans control network traffic
how does connection oriented switching work
subtitle: How Cabletron's connection-oriented switch fabric decided which packets to forward, and which VLANs to forward them within

tldr.problem: A switching fabric has to decide, for every packet, which port it leaves by, and a virtual LAN has to decide which ports may talk to which. Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN product does both with a distributed, connection-oriented design.
tldr.mechanism: Each switch keeps a virtual directory of the whole fabric in its Node and Alias tables. A packet whose source and destination pair is unknown is handed to the base services, which walk it through eight service centers that resolve the address, check the VLAN policy, pick a path and program the connection into the hardware.
tldr.outcome: Once a connection is programmed, the hardware forwards matching packets with no software involvement. The memo documents the model in detail, including the interswitch message protocol used to keep the switches in step.

today: RFC 2643 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a vendor description of a product, written to invite comments, and it describes the SecureFast VLAN operational model rather than a standard others were expected to adopt.

sections.title: The Product and Its Vocabulary
sections.content:
The memo is distributed to the Internet community to solicit reactions to the proposals it contains. Its subject is Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN (SFVLAN) product, which implements a distributed, connection-oriented switching protocol that provides fast forwarding of data packets at the MAC layer.

Within such a network, user traffic is routed through the switch fabric based on the source and destination address pair in the arriving packet. For each pair a switch encounters, a connection is programmed into the switch hardware, mapping the address pair and the port on which the packet arrived to a specific outport. Once a connection exists, all packets with that pair arriving on that port are forwarded by the hardware with no further work.

The memo defines the terms it uses. A switch ID is a 10-octet value that uniquely identifies a switch in the fabric, made of the 6-octet base MAC address of the switch followed by four octets of zeroes; a port ID is the same shape, with the 4-octet local port number of the interface in place of the zeroes. A network port attaches to another switch and an access port attaches to a user endstation. A call connection is the mapping of a source and destination address pair to an inport and outport pair on the switch. A call connection path is the set of 0 to 7 network links over which traffic travels between the source and destination endstations; the paths are chosen from a list of alternate equal cost paths calculated by the VLS protocol, and are chosen to load balance traffic across the fabric. The switch that owns the source endstation is the ingress switch and the one that owns the destination is the egress switch; any others along the path are intermediate switches.

Control traffic has its own vocabulary. The Interswitch Message Protocol (ISMP) is used for communication between SFVLAN switches. Undirected messages are those potentially sent to all switches in the fabric rather than to one switch, and they travel along the switch flood path, a single loop-free path through the fabric built by a spanning tree algorithm that includes only switches running the SFVLAN protocol. A VLAN is a logical grouping of ports and endstations that appear to be on the same LAN segment even when they are geographically separated, and a VLAN identifier is a string of 1 to 16 octets. Each VLAN carries a policy value, and SFVLAN recognises two: Open and Secure.
sections.plainLanguage: The switch keeps a note of every conversation it has seen, pairing the two addresses with the port the packet came in on and the port it should go out on. The hardware then does the forwarding. The rest of the memo describes how those notes are built, kept in step between switches, and filtered by virtual LAN.

sections.title: How VLANs Work Here
sections.content:
Each SFVLAN switch port, and the endstations attached to it, belongs to one or more virtual LANs. VLAN assignments decide whether a requested connection is valid and scope the broadcast of certain flooded messages.

Every port is explicitly assigned to a default VLAN. At start-up the default VLAN for all ports is the base VLAN, a permanent, non-deletable VLAN that every port belongs to at all times. The network administrator can change a port's default VLAN to any other unique VLAN with a management application called the VLAN Manager, and the assignment survives a switch reset. When an endstation attaches to a port for the first time it inherits that port's default VLAN, and the administrator can reassign it later. The memo notes that when all ports and all endstations belong to the base VLAN, the fabric behaves like an 802.1D bridging system.

There are two configuration modes for endstations and two for ports. An endstation is either inherited, meaning it belongs to its port's default VLAN, or static, meaning it belongs to the VLAN the VLAN Manager assigned it; the default for endstations is inherited. A port is either normal, where inherited endstations belong to the port's default VLAN and static endstations to their own assigned VLANs, or locked, where every attached endstation can belong only to the port's default VLAN. The default for ports is normal. The order of precedence matters: on a normal port a static membership beats an inherited one, on a locked port the default VLAN beats any static membership, and if a statically assigned endstation moves from a locked port back to a normal port its static membership must be preserved.

A port can also belong to several VLANs at once, through the membership of its endstations. The memo's example has a port with three endstations, a default VLAN of blue, one endstation statically in red, one statically in green and one inheriting blue. The port is explicitly a member of blue and implicitly a member of red and green, so any tag-based flooding aimed at any of the three VLANs will be forwarded out of that port.
sections.plainLanguage: A port has a home virtual LAN, and anything plugged into it normally joins that LAN too. An administrator can pin a particular computer to a different LAN, or lock the port so that nothing can be pinned anywhere else. A port with computers pinned to several LANs belongs to all of them, which matters when broadcast traffic is sent.

sections.title: The Tag/Length/Value Address Format
sections.content:
Different protocols use different address formats, so many modules inside the product specify addresses in a Tag/Length/Value format. It is a variable-length construct with three parts. The Tag is a 4-octet field giving the type of address contained in the structure. The Value length is a 1-octet field holding the length of the address value, which depends on the address type and the actual value. The Address value is the variable-length field holding the address itself, with its length stored in the Value length field.

The address types supported at the time are listed by tag value: aoMacDx for the DX ethernet destination, source and type; aoIpxSap for SAP; aoIpxRIP for RIP; aoInstYP for the YP name and version; aoInstUDP for a UDP port number; aoIpxIpx for IPX; aoInetIP for an IP network address; aoInetRPC for an RPC program number; aoInetRIP for INET RIP; aoMacDXMcast for a multicast unknown type; aoAtDDP for AppleTalk DDP; aoEmpty when no address type is specified; aoVlan for a VLAN identifier; aoHostName for a host name; aoNetBiosName for a NetBIOS name; aoNBT for a NetBIOS on TCP name; aoInetIPMask for an IP subnet mask; aoIpxSap8022, aoIpxSapSnap and aoIpxSapEnet for the SAP service types; aoDHCPXID for a DHCP transaction identifier; aoIpMcastRx and aoIpMcastTx for an IP class D receiver and sender; aoIpxRip8022, aoIpxRipSnap and aoIpxRipEnet for the IPX RIP service types; aoATM for ATM; and aoATMELAN for an ATM LAN Emulation name.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the product handles several protocols at once, every address is written the same way: a number saying what kind of address it is, a number saying how long it is, and then the address itself.

sections.title: How a Packet Becomes a Connection
sections.content:
The SFVLAN software runs in the switch CPU. The base services handle traffic intercepted by the switch hardware. When a data packet arrives at a local port the hardware examines it, and if the source and destination address pair matches a known connection the hardware simply forwards the packet out the outport the connection specifies. If the pair matches nothing, the hardware diverts the packet to the host control port, where the base services pick it up and create a state box that tracks the progress of the call connection request as it moves through the service centers. The base services check whether the call duplicates one already being processed, and if not they ask the Directory Service Center to add the call's source address to the local Node and Alias tables before handing the call to the Resolve Service Center.

Call connection processing is handled by eight service centers, each with one or more servers, called in a particular sequence, with each server recording its results in the state box and passing the box on. The Directory Service Center catalogues the MAC addresses and alias information for local and remote endstations in two tables: the Node Table holds the MAC addresses of endstations attached to the local switch and a cache of remote endstations, and the Alias Table holds protocol alias information for each endstation, such as an IP or IPX address or a VLAN identifier. The two tables must stay synchronised. The collection of all Node and Alias tables across all switches is the virtual directory of the fabric.

The Resolve Service Center turns the destination address of a broadcast packet, such as an IP ARP packet, into a unicast MAC address. It first tries the local databases: the Table server holds addresses that cannot be resolved in the normal way, such as quiet devices that never send packets or special mappings of IP addresses behind a router; the Local server checks the Node and Alias tables; and, if the address is an IP address that is still not found, the Subnet server applies the subnet mask and looks in the Resolve Table. If the address cannot be resolved locally, the Interswitch Resolve server queries the virtual directory over the switch flood path, and a request that is not answered within 5 seconds is treated as unknown. If the address is unknown everywhere, the Unresolvable server records the packet, the Block server decides whether the address should be added to the Block Table, and the Flood Service Center broadcasts the packet using tag-based flooding.

The remaining service centers do the rest. The Topology Service Center holds the neighbour discovery, spanning tree and link state servers; the link state server runs the VLS protocol to calculate the best paths between the local switch and every other switch, and notifies the Connect Service Center of remote links that have failed. The Policy Service Center decides whether the requested connection is valid from the VLAN policy of the source and destination. The Connect Service Center establishes the connection, the Path Service Center returns up to three best equal-cost paths and the full source-to-destination path as a list of port names, the Filter Service Center programs a connection with no outport, which discards the traffic, and the Flood Service Center broadcasts unresolved packets wrapped in a message carrying the VLAN identifiers of the source endstation.
sections.plainLanguage: When a packet arrives that the hardware does not recognise, the switch software takes over. It looks the destination up in its own tables, then asks the other switches, then works out whether the VLAN rules allow the conversation at all, then picks a route and writes the answer into the hardware so the same packets flow from then on.

sections.title: The Interswitch Message Protocol
sections.content:
ISMP packets are encapsulated in an IEEE 802-compliant frame. The 6-octet destination address holds the MAC address of the multicast channel over which all switches in the fabric receive ISMP packets, which is the value 01-00-1D-00-00-00, except where otherwise noted. The source address holds the physical MAC address of the switch that originated the packet, except where otherwise noted. The 2-octet type field identifies the data carried in the frame and holds the value 0x81FD for ISMP packets.

Two versions of the ISMP packet header are in use. The version 2 header, which this document describes, is 6 octets long and follows the 14-octet frame header: a 2-octet Version field, a 2-octet ISMP message type field, and a 2-octet sequence number used by the protocol handlers for internal synchronisation. The version 3 header is used only by the Interswitch Keepalive message, which is not described here.

The message type tells the switches what to do with the body. The types in use are 3 for the Interswitch Link State message used by the VLS protocol, which is not described in this document; 4 for the Interswitch BPDU message and the Interswitch Remote Blocking message; 5 for the Interswitch Resolve message and the Interswitch New User message; 7 for the Interswitch Tag-Based Flood message; and 8 for the Interswitch Tap/Untap message. Messages of type 5, 7 or 8 are undirected and travel to all switches over the switch flood path. Each switch has at most one upstream neighbour, the switch it receives undirected messages from, and a set of downstream neighbours attached to the other outports of the flood path.
sections.plainLanguage: Switches talk to each other with a protocol of their own, carried in ordinary Ethernet frames addressed to a multicast group so every switch sees it. The message type says what the packet is for, and the flood path is a single loop-free route through the fabric that these broadcasts follow.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo's security section is short. Requested call connections are established or denied based on the VLAN policy of the source and destination addresses specified within the packet, and the section on the policy service center discusses that process in detail. Each VLAN carries a policy value, and SFVLAN recognises two, Open and Secure.

The memo also describes a way to watch traffic. A call tap can be set up on the connection between two endstations, in one or both directions along the connection path, and any switch along that path may request it, once the connection has been established. The probe that receives the copy of the data can be attached to any switch in the topology, so the tap path and the call path may diverge. On each switch along the tap path the tap connection is set up in one of three ways: the existing call connection is used with no modification when the inports and outports match; the existing call connection is modified by enabling an extra outport in one or both directions; or a separate auxiliary connection is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Whether a conversation is allowed comes down to the virtual LAN policy of the two addresses involved. The memo also describes how an operator can watch a connection by tapping it, with the copy collected on any switch in the fabric.

items.label: Interswitch Link State
items.desc: Used by the VLS protocol; not described in this memo.

items.label: Interswitch BPDU
items.desc: Bridge protocol data unit, used by the spanning tree computation.

items.label: Interswitch Remote Blocking
items.desc: Tells a neighbouring switch to stop forwarding on a link.

items.label: Interswitch Resolve
items.desc: Asks the fabric where a destination address lives.

items.label: Interswitch New User
items.desc: Announces a newly attached endstation and asks for its VLAN assignments.

items.label: Interswitch Tag-Based Flood
items.desc: Broadcasts an unresolved packet, scoped by the VLANs of the source.

items.label: Interswitch Tap/Untap
items.desc: Sets up and removes a tap on an existing call connection.
